newsitem.title: UK: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - British business press - Feb 12.

text.p: Prepared for Reuters by The Broadcast Monitoring Company
DAILY TELEGRAPH
AMSTRAD WANTS TO GIVE MILLIONS TO SHAREHOLDERS

Alan Sugar has said that his electronics group, Amstrad, is looking to return most of its 112 million stg cash pile to shareholders. Cash reserves grew by 23 per cent in the six months to last December, and are expected to reach 130 million stg by June. Sugar claims that he had received more acquisition proposals since Psion's attempt at a takeover collapsed last July. He said the Psion talks created a feeling that the group should return value to shareholders.
PLANS TO LET CUSTOMS RAID BANKS HORRIFY ACCOUNTANTS

Accountants have attacked measures contained in the current Finance Bill to allow Customs and Excise to take money directly from a company's bank accounts and customers. David Ratcliffe of the accountancy firm Grant Thornton called it an abuse of power. Roger Gregory of Deloitte & Touche said that the implications could be dreadful. He said that an attachment order could trigger clauses in debenture agreements and tip a business into insolvency. He also claimed it would falsify bank calculations which set off money in one account against an overdraft in another.
VIRTUALITY IN ADMINISTRATION

Administrators have been appointed to the virtual technology company, Virtuality, a week after its shares were suspended pending clarification of its financial position. The move comes four months after Dennis Ohryn, chairman, told the City that the prospects for the company were better than at any time since its floatation. Virtuality was drained of cash after a slump in its arcade machinery business and has just signed a $15 million contract with Philips to license its headsets in the U.S.
THE TIMES
FRESH BLOW FOR SEARS AS FREEMANS SALE REFERRED

Retail company Sears has had its 395 million stg sale of Freemans to Littlewoods referred to the Monopolies and Mergers Commission. The market is concerned it could jeopardise Sears' plans to use the sale proceeds for a share buyback or special dividend and casts further doubts over the future of chief executive Liam Strong. The referral was described by Sears as "disappointing". However, the company remains confident that the deal is not anti-competitive and both companies have reaffirmed their intention to proceed with a sale.
WOOLWICH MEMBERS SUPPORT FLOATATION

A majority of members of the Woolwich Building Society have voted in favour of proposals to convert and float on the stock market. Woolwich held a special general meeting in London to discuss the proposals. Questions raised ranged from concerns about the share distribution to a demand that the Woolwich should not get involved in the transport of land mines after conversion. Investing member Thomas Lines wanted to hear the arguments against conversion in detail, but this was refused by chairman Sir Brian Jenkins.
UNILEVER TO SELL OFF CHEMICALS BUSINESS

The Anglo-Dutch consumer goods group, Unilever, have unveiled plans which could raise up to five billion stg by selling its specialty chemicals business. The money is to be spent on acquisitions in its core areas of food, toiletries and detergents. Chairman Niall Fitzgerald said that the investments would be made in markets where the group was already strong and where it would see growth. He did not rule out returning some cash to shareholders, but only if acquisitions could not be found.
THE GUARDIAN
THE MULTI-MILLION HANDCUFFS

Bert Roberts and Gerry Taylor, the chairman and chief executive of American telecoms group MCI respectively, are set to receive $130 million for their shares and options following the completion of its 12 billion stg takeover by British Telecom . They will both benefit from the multi-million dollar "golden handcuffs" to ensure they stay with the business for at least three years.
TORIES PLANNING LONG LIST OF STATE SELL-OFFS

Chancellor Kenneth Clarke has promised that there will be a new long list of state sell-offs should the Conservatives win the forthcoming general election. This would begin with the privatisation of the national air traffic control service (Nats). He called critics of privatisation in general "selective amnesiacs" and those opposed to the sale of Nats as "scaremongers". He promised that the "long march of privatisation" would go on.
MILLENNIUM BUG MAY BITE DEEP

The inability of many computer systems to cope with the century date change would lead to many companies going bankrupt. Science and technology minister, Ian Taylor, presented a new government survey which showed that only 28 per cent of senior managers were fully aware of the problem. Head of the Government's Year 2000 task force, Robin Guenier, said that many companies had already left it too late to avoid being hit by the problem and the best they could hope for were partial solutions.
THE INDEPENDENT
STRONG STERLING CASTS SHADOW OVER REUTERS

The electronic financial information group, Reuters, has warned that the pound's strength could severely restrict growth prospects, leading to a downgrade in profit forecasts. Chief executive, Peter Job, said that if sterling's strength continues it will restrict prospects for reported revenue and earnings growth in 1997. He warned that moves to offer attractive prices to encourage existing customers to switch to Reuters' new 3000 range of information terminals would have a negative effect on revenue growth this year.
DAVIES SOFTENS STANCE OVER RATES INCREASE

Howard Davies, deputy governor of the Bank of England, has repeated calls for an increase in interest rates. He said that the Bank was not persuaded that on current interest levels it was on track to meet the Government's inflation target of 2.5 per cent over the next two years. However, he added that the rise in rates would be modest in the short term, at a quarter of a per cent. He claims that there is only a small gap between the Bank and the Chancellor on interest rates.
SUMITOMO BID RUMOURS SURROUND LEHMAN BROS

American investment bank Lehman Brothers could be the subject of a buyout bid by Japan's Sumitomo Bank. Lehman is one among several U.S. financial houses being viewed as likely players in a new wave of consolidation on Wall Street in the wake of the Morgan Stanley-Dean Witter merger last week. Sources at Lehman said they had no knowledge of an approach. There is a consensus that Lehman is an attractive target for firms seeking new partners, including banks.
